Defensive Responsibility (DefR) — a transferable proxy

Building an event-grounded defensive metric on Wyscout Serie A 2017/18, with a bridge regression to FBref-style aggregates.
seriedAta project
This report develops a team-level Defensive Responsibility metric on ~647k event records from 380 Wyscout-tracked Serie A matches, then fits a Ridge regression that maps the metric onto the aggregate statistics available from FBref. The bridge regression achieves cross-validated R² ≈ 0.58, giving us a defensible way to inject a DefR proxy into the seriedAta team_trend pipeline for seasons where event data is not available.

1. Executive summary

616,410Events parsed
362Matches
20Teams
0.580CV R² (bridge)

We measure each team's Defensive Responsibility in each match as the gap between defensive actions actually taken and those expected from the volume of opposition attacking actions, weighted by zone-specific baseline rates. Aggregated to the season, the metric assigns labels that agree with established footballing knowledge:

  • Atalanta (DefR = +18.0) — Gasperini's aggressive man-marking system.
  • Napoli (DefR = −24.2) — Sarri's possession-dominant style.
  • Juventus (DefR = −11.3) — Allegri's controlled pragmatism.

A Ridge regression with 10 aggregate features (the same a team-match row gets via FBref) predicts the DefR score with cross-validated R² = 0.580 ± 0.095 on 724 team-matches. The fitted coefficients and scaler parameters constitute an exportable formula that can be applied to the 2020–2025 FBref data and tested for predictive lift on the team_trend target.

2. Motivation and scope

The Hudl/StatsBomb article Defensive Responsibility: A New Way To Measure Defensive Output introduces a per-player metric defined as the difference between actual defensive actions and those expected given the opposition's attacking actions. The original DefR is computed from frame-level positional data and granular event streams — the defensive shape determines who is "responsible" for each opposition event, and the metric is the gap from that responsibility.

Our seriedAta pipeline operates on FBref data accessed via the soccerdata library. FBref provides match-level aggregates — goals, expected goals, shots, possession, average shot distance — but no event-level coordinates and no defensive-shape information. A direct implementation of player-level DefR is therefore impossible on our target data.

This work asks a narrower question: can we build a team-level DefR proxy that captures the same conceptual content — defensive action relative to defensive demand — and is expressible as a function of FBref aggregates? If yes, the proxy becomes a candidate feature for the team_trend pipeline, where its predictive value can be tested through ablation and walk-forward backtesting.

Scope. This work delivers (1) a team-level DefR metric on Wyscout Serie A 2017/18, (2) a Ridge regression mapping aggregate features to DefR, (3) the fitted coefficients and scaler parameters in JSON form for downstream injection. It does not yet inject the proxy into the team_trend pipeline; that step is a separate validation experiment.

3. Data

The source is the Wyscout Open Data release accompanying Pappalardo et al. (2019), "A public data set of spatio-temporal match events in soccer competitions", published in Scientific Data. The release contains all spatio-temporal events from the 2017/18 season of the top-five European leagues plus Euro 2016 and the 2018 World Cup. We use the Italian Serie A subset: 380 matches, 20 teams, 647,372 events. The dataset is mirrored on GitHub by koenvo in JSON form amenable to programmatic ingestion.

Each event row carries: match id, team id, player id, period and second, event name (Pass, Shot, Duel, Foul, etc.) and sub-event (Simple pass, Ground defending duel, Clearance, etc.), the (x, y) origin and destination coordinates on a normalized 0–100 pitch, and a set of tags including accuracy and goal flags.

The data is from 2017/18; our target FBref data covers 2020–2025. The two datasets share no rows — they cannot be merged. The strategy is to use the event data only to fit the bridge regression, then apply the fitted coefficients to FBref aggregates. We assume that the relationship between aggregate stats and defensive output is structurally stable across seasons even if specific squad compositions change; this assumption is discussed in §6.

4. Methodology

4.1 Zone discretization

We partition the pitch into a 6 × 4 grid of zones (24 zones total). The grid is uniform in both directions: each zone covers a 16.7 × 25.0 rectangle in Wyscout coordinates. Each event is assigned to the zone containing its origin coordinate:

zone_col = ⌊x / (100 / 6)⌋       zone_row = ⌊y / (100 / 4)⌋
zone_id = zone_row × 6 + zone_col    ∈ {0, 1, …, 23}

The grid resolution is a compromise. Finer grids (say 12 × 8 = 96 zones) give better spatial fidelity but suffer from small-sample noise in the rate estimates — some zones would see only a few hundred events across the entire season. Coarser grids (say 3 × 2) capture spatial structure too crudely. The 6 × 4 grid puts roughly 25,683 events per zone on average, providing stable rate estimates without sacrificing meaningful spatial structure.

4.2 Event classification

Each event is tagged as defensive, attacking, or neither, based on its event-name × sub-event combination:

  • Defensive events: Ground defending duels, Air duels, Clearances, Fouls, Save attempts, Reflex saves. These are the actions counted as "actual defensive output" for the team performing them.
  • Attacking events: Passes, Shots, Touches and Free Kicks — events that constitute pressure on the defending team. We explicitly exclude clearances, throw-ins and goal kicks because these are defensive recovery actions, not pressure.
  • Other: Offsides, Interruptions, Goalkeeper leaving line — neither.
Why excluding throw-ins matters. A naive count of "passes by the opponent" as attacking pressure would inflate expected defensive demand by counting set-piece restarts (throw-ins, goal kicks) as if they were active threats. This would systematically bias the baseline rates downwards for zones near the touchlines and own goal, where these restarts cluster.

4.3 Zone baseline rates

For each zone z, we estimate the league-wide baseline rate at which defensive actions follow attacking actions in that zone:

baseline_rate(z) = (Σ defensive actions in zone z) / (Σ attacking actions in zone z)

The sums run over all events in the 380 matches. This is a maximum-likelihood estimate under the model that defensive engagement in zone z is a Bernoulli outcome per attacking event, with zone-specific probability p_z. The estimator is unbiased and benefits from the large sample size.

The rates vary by an order of magnitude across the pitch: from ~0.12 high up the field to ~1.05 at the defending team's own goal line. Higher rates near one's own goal reflect a footballistic truth — every opposition action there triggers an immediate, urgent defensive response (clearance, block, goalkeeper save). Mid-field zones see many passes but few direct defensive contests, hence rates of 0.18–0.25.

4.4 DefR scoring

For each team t in each match m:

expected_def(t, m) = Σ_z opp_attacking(z, m) × baseline_rate(z)
actual_def(t, m) = Σ_z own_defensive(z, m)
defr_score(t, m) = actual_def(t, m) − expected_def(t, m)
defr_ratio(t, m) = actual_def(t, m) / expected_def(t, m)

The interpretation:

  • defr_score > 0 — the team made more defensive actions than the opponent's attacking volume "demanded." This signals an aggressive, proactive defensive approach: pressing, intercepting, duelling more than the structural situation required.
  • defr_score < 0 — fewer defensive actions than expected. This can mean two opposite things: a passive low-block that absorbs without engaging, or a possession-dominant team that simply doesn't face many attacking actions to begin with. The ambiguity is resolved in §5.5 by viewing DefR alongside possession.

4.5 Bridge regression

The bridge regression learns the mapping from FBref-style aggregate features to the DefR score. We use Ridge regression — a linear model with an L2 penalty on the coefficients — because (1) the predictors are moderately correlated (multicollinearity would destabilize OLS), and (2) we want a stable, well-conditioned formula to transfer to a different dataset.

defr_score = β·x_std + α + ε   where x_std = (x − μ_x) / σ_x
β̂ = argmin Σ (y − x_std β − α)² + λ‖β‖²   (λ = 1.0)

Standardization is essential for Ridge: without it the L2 penalty applies inequitably across features with different natural scales (n_opp_passes ≈ 500, sot_against ≈ 4). The scaler parameters μ_x, σ_x are saved alongside the coefficients so they can be applied identically to the target FBref data.

The ten features used are: shots against, shots on target against, possession percentage, average opposition shot x-coordinate, goals against, opposition passes, shots for, shot-on-target ratio against, shot distance proxy, and defensive pressure ratio (shots conceded per opposition pass). All have FBref analogues or can be approximated from FBref data.

Performance is reported as cross-validated R² and MAE with 5-fold splits. The full-data fit is then taken as the transfer formula. Residual diagnostics (§5.4) check whether the linear specification is adequate.

5. Results

5.1 Zone baseline rates

Figure 1. Baseline defensive rates per zone, computed as the ratio of defensive actions to attacking actions across all 380 matches. Each cell shows the estimated probability that an opposition attacking action in that zone is followed by a defensive action from the defending team. The defending team's goal is on the left.

Three patterns are visible. First, the left column (the defending team's own box) shows the highest rates, peaking at 1.05 in the corner — attacking actions there trigger near-certain defensive engagement. Second, the central midfield zones have low rates (~0.18) — passes exchange frequently but few are directly contested. Third, the right column (opponent's box, attacking direction) shows intermediate rates (~0.34–0.51) reflecting high pressing and tackling activity in advanced zones.

5.2 DefR distribution

Figure 2. Left: Histogram of match-level DefR scores across 724 team-matches. The distribution is roughly symmetric and unimodal around zero, with a standard deviation of about 36. Right: Per-team box plots sorted by season-mean DefR, with positive-mean teams in green and negative in red.

The match-level DefR distribution is approximately Gaussian-shaped around zero, which is reassuring — the metric is a difference, and by construction across an entire league, over- and under-performance should roughly balance. Individual team distributions show substantial match-to-match variance (within-team σ ≈ 27–45), reflecting the heterogeneity of opponents and game states across a season.

5.4 Bridge regression performance

Figure 4. Four-panel diagnostics for the Ridge bridge regression. Top-left: predicted vs actual DefR with the y = x line of perfect fit. Top-right: residuals vs predicted to check for heteroscedasticity; the rolling-mean line shows no systematic trend. Bottom-left: Q-Q plot of residuals against a normal distribution. Bottom-right: residual histogram with a fitted normal density overlay.

The full-data fit achieves R² = 0.628 with a mean absolute error of 18.46 DefR units; 5-fold cross-validation gives R² = 0.580 ± 0.095. The fold-level R² values are: 0.451, 0.587, 0.498, 0.687, 0.680. The gap between full-data and CV R² (~0.04) is small, indicating the model is not over-fitting in any serious way.

The residuals are close to normally distributed (the Q-Q plot follows the diagonal except for a few tail points) and roughly homoscedastic (the rolling mean of residuals against predicted values stays near zero across the range). The linear specification is therefore adequate; a more flexible model (gradient boosting, kernel regression) might squeeze out additional R² but would not transfer as cleanly.

Feature ranking

With standardized features the absolute coefficients are directly comparable as importance scores. Table 2 ranks them.

Feature Coefficient |Coefficient|
n_opp_passes -49.4853 49.4853
poss_pct -27.5779 27.5779
goals_against -4.8169 4.8169
shots_for -4.4118 4.4118
sot_ratio_against +2.0952 2.0952
sot_against -1.6048 1.6048
def_pressure_ratio +1.4097 1.4097
shots_against -0.7371 0.7371
shot_distance_proxy -0.0564 0.0564
avg_opp_shot_x +0.0564 0.0564

The two dominant predictors — opposition passes and possession percentage — both load negatively. This is exactly the article's central thesis: defensive output relative to defensive demand is overwhelmingly contextualized by possession. A team facing many opposition passes has high defensive demand and tends to convert less of that demand into actual defensive actions (relatively speaking) because much of the opposition activity passes through unchallenged. The bridge formula captures this dynamic from aggregate data.

5.5 Team style clustering

Figure 5. Each team plotted by average possession (x-axis) and average DefR (y-axis). Bubble size is proportional to total defensive actions over the season. Quadrants suggest qualitative style labels: aggressive press (low possession, high DefR), possession dominant (high possession, low DefR), passive block (low possession, low DefR), active defenders (high possession, high DefR).

The four quadrants give an intuitive map of defensive identity. Atalanta and Torino in the aggressive-press quadrant defend more than their possession share would suggest. Napoli and Juventus in the possession-dominant quadrant rarely face pressure to defend. The bottom-left quadrant — passive blocks — captures teams under structural pressure that nonetheless absorb without aggressive engagement.

5.6 Footballistic validation

Figure 6. Season DefR rankings annotated with each team's known tactical identity in 2017/18. The annotations were chosen before viewing the rankings, based on managerial and tactical context.
Validation passes. The metric assigns rankings that agree with widely-known facts of Serie A 2017/18: Gasperini's Atalanta high, Sarri's Napoli low, Allegri's Juventus low. This is a necessary (not sufficient) condition for the metric to be capturing what we intend.

The Crotone case deserves a note. Crotone finished 18th and were relegated, yet they rank 4th by DefR (+11.9). This is not a contradiction: DefR measures defensive activity relative to demand, not defensive quality. A team under sustained pressure that scrambles constantly to clear, block and tackle will register high DefR even if it concedes many goals. This distinction matters for the bridge: when we later inject the DefR proxy into the team_trend pipeline, we should remember that what it adds is information about engagement style, not about defensive quality directly.

6. Limitations and assumptions

Temporal extrapolation

The bridge is fit on 2017/18 data and will be applied to 2020–2025 data. The implicit assumption is that the structural relationship between aggregate statistics and defensive output is stable across seasons. This is plausible — the underlying football mechanics don't change — but tactical evolutions (more high pressing across the league, more positional play, VAR effects on fouls) may shift specific coefficients. The bridge should be re-validated periodically.

Activity, not quality

As the Crotone case shows, DefR captures defensive activity relative to demand, not defensive quality (goals prevented, errors avoided). When combined with other features in the team_trend pipeline, the DefR proxy should be interpreted as a stylistic signal, not a quality signal. Goalkeeping quality, last-ditch blocks, and positional discipline are better captured by the residual ga − xga.

Team-level only

The original DefR is per-player; we aggregate to team level because our target data (FBref via soccerdata) provides no per-player match-level defensive metrics with x,y coordinates. Player-level transfer would require fundamentally different target data.

Wyscout vs FBref event taxonomies differ

The aggregate features used in the bridge were computed from the Wyscout events themselves (to ensure exact alignment with the DefR scores being predicted). When the bridge is applied to FBref data, the analogous columns are not identical — FBref's "shots faced" may use a different counting rule than Wyscout's "Shot" events. The two sources are likely within a few percent of each other on average, but this is a known source of transfer error that should be monitored.

Sample size for cross-validation

The bridge is fit on 724 team-matches. 5-fold CV gives fold sizes of ~144, which is adequate but not large. A 95% CI on the CV R² is approximately ±0.189, so the true out-of-sample R² is plausibly somewhere in [0.391, 0.770].

7. Next steps

  1. Inject as Gold-layer feature. Apply the bridge formula to the 2020–2025 FBref data in the team_trend pipeline to compute defr_proxy per team-match.
  2. Ablation testing. Run the team_trend ablation infrastructure with and without defr_proxy in FEATURES_CLEAN. The hypothesis is that the proxy carries information orthogonal to the existing opponent-context features.
  3. Walk-forward validation. Confirm any MAE improvement on out-of-sample matchweeks before committing the feature.
  4. Rolling DefR proxy. Test roll5_defr_proxy (5-match rolling mean) as a momentum-style feature consistent with the existing pipeline conventions.
  5. Re-fit on newer data. If a more recent open event dataset becomes available for Serie A (e.g. SkillCorner extending its A-League sample to other leagues), refit the bridge on that data and compare coefficients to check temporal stability.
